newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan insists N.Korea nuclear waste deal safe.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan insists N.Korea nuclear waste deal safe.

text.p: Taiwan on Thursday defended its controversial plan to ship nuclear waste to cash-starved North Korea, pledging not to bow to pressure from South Korea.
"The contract is purely a business activity. It will not be stopped because of political interference," the economics ministry said in a statement.

State utility Taiwan Power Co signed a contract on January 11 under which it can ship up to 200,000 barrels of nuclear waste to North Korea, a Stalinist recluse state whose own nuclear programme has been at the eye of a political storm through the 1990s.
Under the contract, Taipower plans to ship 60,000 barrels of waste in the first two years.
Taipower declined to disclose financial terms, but Taiwan media said the utility had agreed to pay impoverished Pyongyang US$1,150 for each barrel it takes.

Seoul, worried that the deal would pollute the Korean peninsula with radioactive waste, planned to send a delegate to Taiwan's economics ministry on Friday to protest the nuclear waste pact, local media said.
Taiwan said South Korea's concern was unwarranted.

"The planned low-radiation waste shipments by Taipower have been solidified and securely packed in steel barrels according to international practices, so there is absolutely no need to worry about pollution," the ministry statement said.
"The deal will be carried out according to relevant regulations in Taiwan, North Korea and the international community," it said. "It will not cause any negative impact in the Korean peninsula."
South Korea's foreign ministry has voiced "deep regret" over the deal and urged Taiwan not to go ahead with the contract.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with either North Korea or South Korea, which both recognise the rival communist Chinese government in Beijing.
North Korea's nuclear power programme caused international uproar in the early 1990s. The United States and others alleged the programme aimed to develop nuclear weapons.
A key concern was the lack of international inspections.
Pyongyang agreed to freeze and eventually junk the programme in a 1994 pact with Washington, which would reciprocate with US$4.5 billion in safer nuclear technology and interim energy.
Since 1982, Taiwan has stored 97,672 barrels of nuclear waste at Lanyu, just short of its 98,112-barrel capacity.
Taipower has pledged to remove all nuclear waste from Lanyu by 2002 and has been seeking sites overseas, including China, the Marshall Islands and Russia.
Taiwan has three nuclear power plants in operation and a fourth under construction in northern Taipei county.
